claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an fcc matrix.
The starting alloy has demonstrated high strength and fatigue performance.
High-temperature degradation in both oxidizing and reducing atmospheres is controlled by selective oxidation or reduction kinetics of Al, Cr, and Ti.
Al, Cr, and Ti form a dynamic, thin oxide scale on the alloy.
Oxide-scale formation, adhesion, and breakdown directly govern degradation.
Oxide-scale evolution occurs without destabilizing the fcc matrix.
Marginal changes in Al, Cr, and Ti concentrations can modify selective oxidation or reduction kinetics.
Transient Al-, Cr-, and Ti-derived surface oxides act as diffusion barriers between the environment and the fcc matrix.
At high temperature, Al, Cr, and Ti preferentially oxidize.
Reducing conditions may prevent formation or persistence of protective oxide layers.
Oxide-scale formation, adhesion, and growth are governed by diffusion kinetics and synergistic interactions among Al, Cr, and Ti.
A continuous, adherent oxide scale protects the alloy matrix, whereas a less effective scale accelerates degradation.
Compositions favoring a continuous, adherent scale will show reduced mass gain and better retention of mechanical properties under oxidizing conditions.
The protective benefit of favorable Al, Cr, and Ti tuning will diminish under reducing atmospheres, and degradation may become more pronounced.
Marginally reducing the concentrations of the key reactive elements will produce less protective oxide behavior and faster degradation.
Oxidation behavior in high-entropy alloys depends strongly on alloy composition and testing conditions.
The relevant exposure boundary for testing this hypothesis is 800–1000 °C.
The compositional modifications can be kept marginal enough to preserve the fcc matrix while isolating oxidation or reduction kinetics.
